newsitem.title: INDIA: India on course for growth despite hiccup - analysts.
newsitem.headline: India on course for growth despite hiccup - analysts.

text.p: The Indian economy is shrugging off a worrisome slowdown that was reflected by dismal data released last week, and is on course for steady growth, analysts said on Monday.

They said a new tax-cutting budget and a more relaxed credit policy had set in motion a fresh wave of economic buoyancy that belied a sharp slowdown in exports, imports and industrial growth in the financial year ended March 31.

India last week said exports in 1996/97 edged up 4.01 percent over the previous year, after a spurt of 21.38 percent growth in 1995/96. Imports grew by barely six percent, pointing to sluggish demand for intermediate and capital goods.

The government said industrial output in January crawled ahead by 1.1 percent against 12.9 percent in the same monh in 1996. Industrial output grew at just 7.5 percent in the first 10 months of 1996/97, compared with 11.7 percent in the corresponding period the previous year.

"These figures just confirm that last year there was an industrial slowdown. The government has since taken steps to restore business confidence. It means nothing more than that," said Tushar Sarda, head of Daewoo Securities in India.
"One important factor was the availability of money and interest rates. But the new credit policy has taken care of that," Sarda said.
The Reserve Bank of India, the nation's central bank, last month announced an array of steps to bolster funds available with commercial banks for lending and to cut lending rates.
"It (1996/97) was a difficult year, especially in the first half, when interest rates were very high," said Shashanka Bhide of New Delhi's National Council for Applied Economic Research.
"The interest rate scenario has improved substantially now. I would think investment expenditure would recover and rise significantly this year," Bhide told Reuters.
Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram says the economy should grow at least seven percent in 1997/98. The government has projected a 12 percent industrial output growth rate.
"Seven to eight percent GDP (gross domestic product) growth now does not seem difficult," Sarda told Reuters. "I believe the government is very serious about economic growth and liberalisation."
India's lower house of parliament last week approved a raft of tax-cutting and economic liberalisation proposals that Chidambaram included in his budget for 1997/98.
The new laws sweep away a painful surcharge on corporate profits and a tax on income from dividends. They also lower the tax rate on corporate profits and personal income.
Bhide said the budget proposals had sparked a flurry of economic activity after a lean business period.
"Both in terms of tax measures and credit policy, the investment climate has improved substantially," Bhide said.
"A new government in place will help political stability as well. For the year, the scenario is now set."
